body:
STAGE 1: USER INPUT
AudioEval takes a monophonic clarinet recording and its intended MusicXML score. The recording provides evidence of what was played; the score specifies what was intended. Each score event stores written pitch, onset, duration, measure, part and a unique index. Tied notes form one sustained event, while separately articulated notes keep distinct identities even when their pitches match. Ornament markings remain available for alignment.

Audio is converted to mono at 22,050 Hz. The deployed model expects written B-flat-clarinet pitches, two semitones above sounding pitch. Concert-pitch scores therefore require conversion. Analysis uses only the recording and reference score, without the known correspondences available during synthetic training.

STAGE 2: TRANSCRIPTION
The current neural transcriber uses two log-mel spectrograms. A long window preserves pitch structure, while a short window captures attacks and brief notes. They use 2,048- and 512-sample windows and advance together every 256 samples, approximately 11.61 ms. Convolutional encoders combine both views, and temporal convolution blocks add surrounding context.

Connectionist temporal classification (CTC) predicts an ordered pitch sequence without requiring exact note-duration targets. Additional outputs estimate voicing, attacks, boundaries, rearticulation and confidence. Training targets describe the notes actually rendered, including errors and repeat copies, so the network learns the performed sequence rather than the clean score.

Decoding retains candidate pitches, onset times, confidence and supported alternatives. Optional candidates can be accepted or rejected during alignment; short duration alone does not justify rejection. Postprocessing uses energy and spectral continuity to distinguish duplicate emissions from genuine same-pitch attacks. The experimental v10 extension can restore an already decoded boundary, then realign under a consistency check. It does not invent onsets.

STAGE 3: ALIGNMENT
A recording may cover only part of a piece. The passage locator uses confidence-weighted subsequence edit distance to find plausible score regions. Material before and after the attempted passage is not automatically labelled missing. Up to four candidate passages are retained, each extended by eight context notes at both ends.

For each passage, a template without a restart competes with bounded repeat and ornament templates. Notes retain their original score identity plus an occurrence index. For example, a performance of 1-2-3-2-3-4 can represent a replay of score notes 2-3 before continuing to note 4. Both visits refer to the same written notes but different recording intervals.

Dynamic programming compares pitch matches, substitutions, insertions, deletions and rejection of unreliable candidates. Supported alternative pitches can also be selected. Confidence affects the configured edit costs, and a penalty discourages unnecessary repeat copies. Unlike the earlier learned path scorer, this search uses explicit costs and does not support arbitrary nested repeats or unrestricted jumps.

Confident matches anchor a score-to-recording time map. With at least four anchors, a second pass adds a capped onset-deviation cost to refine ambiguous matches while allowing expressive timing. If several passages remain plausible, the current system selects the earliest qualifying location and records the ambiguity.

STAGE 3.1: NOTE ERROR LABELLING
A pitch substitution at an original score occurrence becomes a wrong-note label. An unexplained retained candidate is a possible extra note; an unfilled score event is a possible omission. Repeat identities generate a separate repetition label, preventing a replay from being treated simply as many extra notes.

Separate classifiers verify extra and missed proposals using acoustic support, duration, nearby alignment, timing and structural context. A missed-note verifier also examines the spectrogram near the expected onset for the intended pitch, checking whether transcription overlooked a played note. Weakly supported decisions are withheld. The current exporter does not report separate content errors inside replayed copies.

STAGE 3.2: RHYTHM ERROR LABELLING
This branch belongs to the earlier system shown in the diagram. It estimates tempo from the candidate recording span and score duration, then expresses note durations and spacing relative to that scale. Its rhythm classifier uses a threshold of 0.5 in the reported evaluation.

The current revision uses onset timing to improve alignment but does not emit rhythm-error labels. It also does not assess intonation or timbre. The historical rhythm results therefore do not validate these capabilities in the revised method.

STAGE 4: LABEL OUTPUT
Each label links an error type to affected score-note identities, contextual notes and a recording interval. Extra notes attach to neighbouring score events. Missed-note replay times are estimated from surrounding aligned onsets or a tempo map, with an explicit unavailable state when estimation fails. Repetition labels include the original interval, replay interval and additional-copy count.

A practice interface can highlight the affected notes and replay their audio. Poor alignment support, failed passage retrieval or search limits can produce an uncertain result with withheld labels. Unplayed passages and withheld decisions remain unassessed; an empty error list does not prove a clean performance.
intro: The diagram organises AudioEval into input, transcription, alignment, error labelling and feedback. It depicts the earlier system, including its rhythm branch. The explanations below describe the current method within these modules and identify the historical components. The reported experimental results evaluate earlier configurations; they do not establish the accuracy of the revised pipeline.
